description: React's process of attaching event handlers and client-side state to server-rendered HTML, making the static markup interactive. In Next.js App Router, hydration applies only to Client Components. The server-rendered HTML must be byte-for-byte consistent with the initial client render output — any mismatch is a hydration error.
constraints: Server-rendered HTML output of a Client Component must exactly match its initial client-rendered output
Dynamic values that differ between server and client (Date.now(), Math.random(), browser dimensions) must not be rendered during SSR if they differ from the client value
Hydration applies only to Client Components — Server Components are not hydrated (they have no client-side React lifecycle)
The client JavaScript bundle must be downloaded and parsed before hydration can begin
useLayoutEffect is deferred until after hydration on the client — server emits a warning if used where SSR output would differ
Components using browser APIs (window, document) must be guarded with typeof window !== 'undefined' or mounted-state checks if rendered during SSR
React context consumed in Client Components must receive the same initial value on server and client
allowedPatterns: Rendering static, deterministic content on the server that is identical to the client's initial render
Using suppressHydrationWarning on elements with known intentional server/client differences (e.g. browser extension injected attributes)
Deferring browser-API-dependent rendering to useEffect (runs only after hydration) or to a mounted state flag
Using React.lazy() with Suspense to defer hydration of non-critical interactive components
Using dynamic() with ssr: false for components that are entirely incompatible with SSR
Wrapping dynamic values in useEffect to update after hydration without causing mismatch
Using the React use() API with a promise passed from a Server Component to stream and hydrate data progressively
forbiddenPatterns: Rendering Date.now() or new Date() directly in JSX of a Client Component — server and client timestamps differ
Rendering Math.random() or crypto.randomUUID() inline in JSX — produces different values on server and client
Accessing window, document, or screen properties during the render phase of a Client Component
Rendering different content based on typeof window check during the render phase — produces HTML that mismatches client output
Using localStorage or sessionStorage during render — not available during server-side prerender
Mutating the DOM directly during render — bypasses React's reconciliation and breaks hydration
Importing and using browser-only libraries at module scope in Client Components that are SSR'd
runtimeBehavior: Step 1 (server): Client Components are prerendered into static HTML — React runs once to produce markup, no event handlers
Step 2 (client, first load): Browser receives HTML and displays it immediately as non-interactive content (FCP)
Step 3 (client): RSC Payload is used to reconcile the Server and Client Component trees
Step 4 (client): React downloads Client Component JavaScript chunks and executes them
Step 5 (client): React 'hydrates' the existing HTML by attaching event handlers and initializing state — DOM is not re-created
If server HTML matches client output exactly: hydration is silent and seamless
If server HTML does NOT match client output: React logs a hydration mismatch warning in development and attempts recovery in production — may cause visual flicker or incorrect UI state
Hydration happens synchronously from the root — blocking the main thread during processing
Streaming partial hydration: Suspense boundaries allow progressive hydration — each boundary hydrates independently as its content arrives
Subsequent client-side navigations: Client Components are rendered entirely on client without SSR — hydration only occurs on first load or full page refresh
architectureImplications: Server Components are never hydrated — they have no client runtime cost after initial HTML delivery
Minimizing Client Component surface area directly reduces hydration work and Time to Interactive (TTI)
Suspense boundaries create independent hydration units — use them to defer hydration of below-the-fold content
The RSC Payload is the mechanism that allows React to hydrate without re-fetching server data
dynamic({ ssr: false }) completely removes a component from SSR and hydration — use for browser-only widgets
next/dynamic with ssr: false increases FCP for the deferred component — trade-off between SSR consistency and compatibility
Hydration errors in production are difficult to detect without monitoring — they may silently produce incorrect UI
performanceImplications: Hydration blocks interactivity — Time to Interactive (TTI) is delayed until all Client Component JS is parsed and hydration completes
Large Client Component trees with many event handlers increase hydration duration
Streaming with Suspense enables partial hydration — above-the-fold content becomes interactive before below-the-fold content is even received
Reducing Client Component count and size directly reduces hydration cost
dynamic() with lazy loading defers JS download until needed — reduces initial bundle but delays hydration of the lazy component
Hydration mismatch recovery is expensive — React re-renders the mismatched subtree on the client
RSC Payload size directly affects client navigation performance — large Server Component trees produce larger payloads
commonMisusePatterns: Rendering new Date().toLocaleDateString() in a Client Component without accounting for timezone/locale differences between server and client
Using Math.random() to generate element keys or IDs in JSX — different on each render, causes mismatch
Checking typeof window !== 'undefined' to conditionally render content — returns false on server, true on client, guarantees mismatch
Reading localStorage or cookies directly during render instead of in useEffect
Using a third-party library that accesses window at import time without wrapping in dynamic({ ssr: false })
Not suppressing hydration warnings on elements intentionally different (e.g. elements modified by browser extensions)
Assuming useLayoutEffect behavior is consistent between server and client — it is suppressed on server and fires synchronously after paint on client
productionRisks: Silent UI corruption: hydration mismatches in production do not throw — React attempts to recover, potentially leaving the UI in an incorrect state that is invisible to developers
Visual flicker: mismatch recovery causes a visible re-render flash on first load, degrading perceived performance
SEO impact: crawlers see server HTML; if hydration alters content, the visible and indexed content diverge
Time to Interactive regression: oversized client bundles from unnecessary Client Component usage delay hydration and TTI
Hydration errors in deeply nested components are hard to trace — the error message often points to the root boundary, not the offending component
Browser extension interference: extensions that inject attributes or text nodes into the DOM cause spurious hydration warnings — suppressHydrationWarning is the correct mitigation
